strengths: Addresses a critical and practical bottleneck in diffusion-based video super-resolution (VSR): scaling to long-form videos with streaming inference, constant GPU memory overhead, and single-step speed.

Well-crafted technical design combining a dual-timescale modeling strategy (rolling KV-cache for local continuity and LR keyframe visual prompting for global identity preservation) with memory-efficient training techniques (patch-wise latent decoding and cross-chunk distribution matching).

Introduces MovieLQ, a 1000-frame real-world long-video benchmark, and sensibly integrates VBench semantic consistency metrics (subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness) alongside standard perceptual and pixel-level IQA metrics.

Comprehensive experimental results demonstrating substantial inference speedups (up to 58x faster than MGLD-VSR and over 5x faster than SeedVR2) while retaining constant 20.4 GB peak memory and competitive-to-superior perceptual quality.
weaknesses: Certain details regarding the cross-chunk distribution matching (DMD) setup are underspecified, particularly the exact architecture and checkpoint of the teacher video model, as well as the exact computational cost and stability of Stage II training with 3-chunk rollouts.

The 3D VAE decoder includes spatio-temporal convolutions; spatially cropping latents prior to decoding ($D(C_{\text{lat}}(\hat{z}))$) can introduce boundary padding discrepancies compared to decoding the full latent and then cropping. The potential impact of this approximation on spatial boundary quality during training should be clarified.

Handling of scene cuts or multi-shot videos is not explicitly addressed: a static global visual prompt extracted from a single keyframe and an uninterrupted rolling KV-cache could cause ghosting or identity bleed across major scene transitions.

While perceptual metrics (DOVER, CLIPIQA) and speed are superior, fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are lower than some full-sequence baselines (e.g., SeedVR2 on UDM10 and SPMCS); a deeper discussion analyzing this perception-fidelity trade-off would be beneficial.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and practical bottleneck in diffusion-based video super-resolution (VSR): scaling to long/unbounded sequences with bounded memory and high inference speed.
Well-motivated architecture combining intra-chunk single-step diffusion with inter-chunk autoregressive generation using a rolling KV-cache and global LR visual prompts.
Clever training formulation: patch-wise pixel supervision effectively mitigates the heavy memory overhead of 3D VAE decoding, enabling efficient high-resolution training on standard hardware.

Extensive experimental validation across both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating competitive quality, constant memory footprint across sequence lengths, and up to 58x speedup over multi-step diffusion baselines.
Introduction of MovieLQ (1000-frame benchmark) and the incorporation of semantic-level consistency metrics (VBench) provide valuable evaluation assets for the community.
weaknesses: The formulation and implementation details of the cross-chunk distribution matching loss (Eq. 6) are somewhat high-level; further specifics on the teacher model, the exact score distillation gradient formulation, and noise scheduling across chunks would improve technical clarity and reproducibility.

Lack of temporal degradation/drift analysis across very long videos: while evaluated on 1000-frame sequences, the paper does not show how metrics (e.g., fidelity or drift) evolve as a function of frame/chunk index over time to quantify compounding autoregressive errors.

Reliance on a single global reference frame (e.g., the middle frame) for cross-attention guidance may struggle with videos containing substantial appearance changes, complex object occlusions, or camera scene transitions.

strengths: Practical and timely formulation: Reformulating diffusion-based video super-resolution into an autoregressive one-step diffusion (AR-OSD) framework effectively tackles both memory explosion and high inference latency on long sequences.

Substantial efficiency gains: The proposed framework operates with constant peak GPU memory over time and delivers dramatic acceleration (e.g., 6.82s for 33 frames at 720p, roughly 58x faster than MGLD-VSR and over 5x faster than SeedVR2) while maintaining high perceptual quality.

Thoughtful architectural adaptations: The combination of rolling KV-cache for local continuity, joint visual prompt guidance for global identity anchoring, and patch-wise pixel supervision to bypass 3D VAE decoding memory constraints is well-designed and technically sound.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and new benchmark: The paper evaluates on five benchmarks, introduces the 1000-frame MovieLQ dataset to address the lack of long-form VSR evaluation, and incorporates semantic consistency metrics (VBench) alongside pixel-level warping errors.
weaknesses: Lack of temporal drift curves over long sequences: While MovieLQ comprises 1000 frames, only sequence-averaged metrics are reported. There is no frame-by-frame analysis (e.g., PSNR/LPIPS/E_warp plotted across time) to demonstrate whether autoregressive error accumulation or subtle semantic drift occurs over hundreds of consecutive rollout steps.

Handling of multi-shot videos and anchor selection: The global guidance relies on visual prompts extracted from LR key frames (e.g., the middle frame). The paper does not clarify how this mechanism behaves under scene transitions, camera cuts, or significant appearance changes where a single static anchor frame is invalid.

Underspecified distribution matching distillation (DMD) formulation: Section 3.3 presents Eq. (6) at a very high level, omitting crucial implementation details regarding the exact teacher model checkpoint, how score differences are computed across the 3-chunk window, and whether gradients are backpropagated through previous cache states.

Trade-off between perceptual metrics and pixel fidelity: As typical in generative restoration, the method exhibits lower PSNR/SSIM compared to some non-generative or earlier regression-based baselines (e.g., RealViFormer, SeedVR2). A more detailed discussion on the distortion-perception trade-off and hallucination behavior would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge: scaling generative video super-resolution to long, arbitrary-length sequences under fixed memory and low latency constraints.

Well-motivated technical design combining an autoregressive one-step diffusion formulation with a rolling KV-cache and joint visual guidance, which effectively preserves both local continuity and global semantic consistency.

Clever training efficiency strategy: the patch-wise pixel supervision avoids the prohibitive memory overhead of 3D VAE decoding on full video volumes, enabling effective high-resolution training on modest hardware (4 A800 GPUs).

Impressive efficiency gains demonstrated empirically, achieving up to 58x speedup over multi-step diffusion baselines like MGLD-VSR and over 5x over single-step baselines like SeedVR2, while maintaining constant peak memory over long sequences.
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse synthetic and real-world benchmarks, incorporating both low-level temporal warping error and high-level semantic temporal consistency metrics from VBench.
weaknesses: The newly introduced MovieLQ benchmark is relatively small in scale, consisting of only 10 video sequences, which limits its statistical coverage of diverse real-world motion patterns and scene categories.

Certain operational details of the joint visual guidance module, such as the exact mathematical criterion and threshold for triggering key-frame switching during motion or scene changes, are not fully formalized in the main text.

While perceptual and temporal metrics are strong, there is a visible trade-off against traditional pixel-level reconstruction fidelity (e.g., PSNR/SSIM compared to SeedVR2 or RealViFormer on UDM10/SPMCS), which is common in generative super-resolution but warrants more explicit analysis regarding texture hallucination versus true signal recovery.

strengths: Well-motivated and effective framework: Formulating long-form generative VSR as an autoregressive one-step diffusion (AR-OSD) process with a rolling KV-cache and causal VAE cleanly resolves memory explosion and boundary discontinuities in streaming scenarios.

Efficient high-resolution training: The proposed patch-wise pixel supervision cleverly sidesteps the prohibitive memory overhead of full 3D VAE decoding during training, enabling effective fine-tuning on high-resolution data with modest hardware resources (4 A800 GPUs).

Strong efficiency and throughput: InfVSR achieves constant memory scaling over sequence length and a significant speedup (e.g., 6.82s for 33 frames of 720p, achieving over 58x speedup compared to MGLD-VSR and more than 5x over SeedVR2).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The manuscript evaluates extensively across multiple synthetic and real-world datasets, validates temporal consistency at both pixel (warping error) and semantic (VBench metrics) levels, and provides clear ablations for all core components (cache size, guidance, DMD, curriculum).
weaknesses: Limited size of the proposed MovieLQ benchmark: While introducing 1000-frame evaluation sequences fills an important gap in long-form VSR, the MovieLQ dataset comprises only 10 clips, which is relatively small to capture diverse scene dynamics and degradation variations.

Handling of shot transitions: The streaming mechanism relies primarily on external scene detection (PySceneDetect, discussed in Appendix A.3) to reset KV caches across shot cuts, rather than handling transitions intrinsically within the model architecture.

Trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality: On several synthetic benchmarks (e.g., UDM10, SPMCS), traditional full-reference fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are lower than some baselines such as SeedVR2, reflecting the typical generative trade-off that should be explicitly contextualized.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: The paper tackles a significant bottleneck in generative video super-resolution (VSR)—namely, the severe memory footprint and boundary inconsistency that occur when processing extended video sequences with diffusion models.

Well-motivated technical design: Reformulating VSR into an autoregressive one-step diffusion (AR-OSD) framework with causal DiT adaptations (rolling KV-cache and LR-based joint visual guidance) allows for true streaming inference with bounded memory and linear runtime scaling.

Efficient and principled training scheme: The combination of patch-wise pixel supervision (avoiding heavy full-frame 3D VAE decoding during backpropagation) and cross-chunk distribution matching ($L_{\text{DMD}}$) enables effective training under accessible hardware budgets (4 A800 GPUs).

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across five benchmarks (UDM10, SPMCS, MVSR4x, VideoLQ, and the newly established 1000-frame MovieLQ). It shows significant speedups (up to 58× over multi-step MGLD-VSR and over 5× over SeedVR2) while retaining constant GPU memory and competitive or superior visual/temporal metrics.

Thorough ablation studies: The ablations convincingly justify key design choices, including rolling KV-cache vs. independent chunking/aggregation, KV-cache lengths, joint visual guidance, patch supervision, and temporal regularization objectives.
weaknesses: Potential boundary artifacts in patch-wise 3D VAE decoding: The patch-wise pixel supervision decodes a cropped latent region $h \times w$ using the 3D VAE decoder. Because spatial/temporal convolutions and padding in 3D VAEs rely on spatial context, cropping latents independently can introduce boundary discrepancy compared to decoding full latent frames; this potential artifact is neither analyzed nor discussed.

Heuristic details for visual guidance switching: Section 3.2 states that reference key-frame prompts are switched 'when large motion or low reference relevance is detected', but the exact metric, threshold criteria, and sensitivity analysis for this triggering mechanism are under-specified in the main text.

Limited size of the MovieLQ benchmark: While MovieLQ provides valuable long-sequence testing (1000 frames per video), the benchmark contains only 10 video clips. Expanding the diversity of scenes, motions, and degradation profiles would make it a more authoritative benchmark.
